items.title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.original_title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.rss_title: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy
items.rss_description: How Gen AI Can Help Shape Strategy PaulCarroll Mon, 11/02/2026 - 11:30 Bill Gates recently said he is using generative AI as part of the annual, two-week strategy session that determines how the Gates Foundation spends its next $10 billion. He'll be "taking the strategy notes and actually engaging in a dialogue with ChatGPT, Claude, Copilot, and even having them talk with each other," he said. I don't have $10 billion that I'm considering how to spend, and you may not, either, but genAI has now improved to the point where it can at least be an aid in setting strategy at almost any level. An old boss, Mel Bergstein, used to say: "Strategy is what you don't do." The idea worked for Mel, who founded a consulting firm, Diamond Management & Technology Partners, that pioneered the notion of digital strategy in the mid-1990s. Chunka Mui and I took Mel's adage further in our book, "Billion Dollar Lessons," for which we had 20 researchers spend two years looking at 2,500 major failures to identify the warning signs. Our recommended solution boiled down to having a "devil's advocate" identify all the underlying assumptions for a strategy, to keep problems from being glossed over as an executive team rushed to realize the CEO's plan. GenAI, used right, can now do a pretty good job of filling that role for anyone. Let's have a look. Gates told the New York Times that, "i n a few of the reviews, we’ll actually have the A.I. sit in. In a few cases, we’ll tell it: Hey, only speak if we ask you. And then in a few other cases, we’ll say: Hey, if you hear something you think is wrong or you hear us thinking about, for example, what are these statistics? Please engage. So we’ve gone from it being a joke [when someone suggested using genAI a year ago] to it will be a peer — not making any final decisions, but it will be a peer in deep, complex strategic discussions, making a significant contribution." I'm not willing to go that far just yet, partly because I'd need to test the domain knowledge that the large language models have about a subtle, heavily regulated business like insurance and partly because genAI has shown itself to be a sycophant. The biggest, overarching pattern of failure that Chunka and I found in the research for " Billion Dollar Lessons " was that people were reluctant to point out obvious problems that could derail initiatives that had the imprimatur of the CEO, and we don't want to replace human sycophants with AI ones. But you can describe your strategy to an AI, then pepper it with questions, going deeper each time while demanding evidence for its thinking and insisting it be blunt. Let's say you're thinking of buying a company. You could start with a general question: What could go wrong? Then you probe. How will our competitors react? What if interest rates increase? The economy goes into recession? The war in Iran escalates? Will we actually be able to cross-sell to our customers? Will the efficiencies from scale be as great as we expect? Who's done something similar and had problems? What were the problems? And on and on and on. You can do the same exercise if you're thinking of a new line of business, a software overhaul, adopting AI chatbots — or if you want to explore the dangers of standing pat, of not undertaking a major initiative that is under consideration. Major corporations have staff do extensive analysis along the lines I'm suggesting and, in the case of a possible acquisition, draw on their investment banks for advice — but the bias is always toward acting. If the perception is that the CEO backs an idea, the staff strives to make it work, not to kill it. Investment banks only collect their hefty fees if the deal happens, so why would they recommend against it? When Chunka and I did a consulting project with a major company that was considering launching autonomous vehicles, we saw elaborate studies it had commissioned from consulting firms that said the robotaxi business was a slam dunk and that the first to enter would win big. That was more than eight years ago. It turned out, however, that the executives working on the AV project internally were aware of all the sorts of operational and safety issues that we've all seen play out and that have slowed the robotaxi rollout. Those concerns were brought to the surface in the interviews for our devil's advocate review. Warren Buffett used to set aside two, equal pots of money when asking investment banks for advice on possible acquisitions — one for a bank that argued in favor of a deal and one for a bank that argued against it. Whichever carried the day collected its fees, while the other got nothing. You can be sure the "anti" bank worked as hard as possible on its arguments and evidence. In my experience, many big ideas should fall apart at the slightest scrutiny. As we wrote in "Billion Dollar Lessons," we thought 47% of the failures we investigated were based on strategies that never should have made it out of the strategy room — and not because those involved were stupid or inexperienced. The fifth-biggest cement maker in the world reasoned that it was really in the home products business because so much of its cement was used there. It began also making furnaces and lawn mowers... then went bankrupt and was bought by a competitor. Avon decided that its core competency was its culture of caring — not, you know, its line of cosmetics and its devoted salesforce — so it bought a maker of medical equipment and an operator of retirement homes. It had no idea how to operate the new businesses and quickly sold them at a major loss. In the early days of fax machines, FedEx spent hundreds of millions of dollars to set up a business that would collect a document from you, drive it to the nearest office, fax it to the office nearest your destination, then drive the fax to the recipient. The company somehow missed that Moore's law would soon make the devices so inexpensive that every company would have its own. It may take time to learn how to use genAI to avoid costly strategic mistakes — and that's even before we start using it as broadly as Gates is planning to. You'll likely also need to introduce to the LLM information specific to your market, including regulatory issues that it likely doesn't have even as these models try to Hoover up everything available on the internet. Insurance is a complicated market. But I think we're now at the point where genAI can, if managed correctly, start to catch strategic errors. We won't get that 47% figure for obviously bad ideas down to zero, but even heading toward 40%, maybe even 33%, would mark real progress. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll At any level of setting strategy, from the boardroom to the one-person agency, generative AI can bring assumptions to the surface, helping you see what NOT to do. items.title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.original_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_title: Why Can't We Fund Prevention?
items.rss_description: Why Can't We Fund Prevention? Predict & Prevent ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 09:29 Industrial organizations excel at financing recovery from asset failures but struggle to justify prevention spending with the same economic rigor. November 5, 2026 Image We've built an extraordinarily sophisticated financial system around industrial failure. We can price it, insure it, reserve capital for it, and finance recovery when it happens, but preventing that same failure often requires an entirely different standard of proof. Insurance is exceptionally good at mobilizing money after something goes wrong. Natural catastrophes caused an estimated $100 billion in economic losses in the first half of 2026. Insurance covered approximately 42%, leaving nearly $60 billion to be absorbed elsewhere. Insurance's ability to fund recovery is indispensable. The shortfall also exposes a contradiction in how risk is funded. Premiums, deductibles, and recovery costs have established places in corporate budgets. A proposal to prevent an asset failure faces a tougher test. Someone must prove the threat is serious, determine what intervention it warrants, and defend spending money on an event that might never happen. Failure has a funding mechanism. Prevention has a business case to make. Insurance can transfer part of a financial loss. It cannot restore missed production, repair damaged customer relationships, or undo the wider consequences of an industrial disruption. The challenge is making prevention as intelligible and investable as recovery. Knowing the risk isn't the same as managing it Industrial organizations rarely lack information. They receive risk-engineering reports, inspection findings, maintenance records and alerts from connected equipment. Yet information doesn't guarantee action. A temperature change, unusual vibration, or a deteriorating component has little meaning in isolation. Its significance depends on the asset's role in the operation. Is there redundancy? What production depends on it? What would a shutdown cost? Could a failure disrupt customers, supply chains or other facilities? These questions turn technical observations into business consequences. Without that translation, recommendations can remain in reports while maintenance teams address more immediate demands and capital committees fund projects with clearer returns. Industry has invested heavily in detecting changing conditions and predicting potential failures. Those capabilities matter. Still, knowing what might fail doesn't tell an organization which emerging risks deserve attention first. A relatively minor condition on a critical asset may represent far greater exposure than a severe condition on equipment with sufficient redundancy. The challenge is understanding what matters most, what the consequences could be, and where intervention will create the greatest value. Prevention needs to compete for capital Consider a manufacturer that identifies deterioration in a critical component on its main production line. Although the component hasn't failed, its condition is changing. The organization must compare the cost of replacing it during a planned shutdown with the lost output, repair time, and disruption that could follow an unplanned failure. The consequences, however, may extend well beyond that production line. A shutdown could affect customer deliveries, contractual commitments, supply-chain continuity and financial performance. What appears to be a maintenance decision may represent a much larger business risk. The appropriate response might be immediate repair, closer monitoring, a change in operating parameters or acceptance of the exposure. Someone must have the authority to make that decision and commit the necessary resources before the opportunity to intervene passes. Now multiply that challenge across hundreds of assets and facilities, each presenting different levels of exposure. The question is no longer simply whether an individual intervention is justified. It's which interventions deserve priority when resources are limited, and the consequences extend across the enterprise. For decades, industry has developed sophisticated ways to measure losses after they occur. We need comparable discipline in understanding the economic value of preventing those losses before they happen. Capital should not only be deployed to absorb loss. It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. Andy Pruett

It should be possible to direct it intelligently toward preventing loss. The standard for resilience must rise Risk assessments, inspections and engineering recommendations are essential. Completing those processes, however, doesn't necessarily mean an organization has addressed its most consequential exposures. An inspection can establish that a process was followed. A risk assessment can document a vulnerability. Neither, by itself, demonstrates that the organization is becoming more resilient. Industrial risk isn't static. Asset conditions change, operational dependencies evolve, and an exposure that appeared manageable during a periodic assessment may become significantly more consequential. A recommendation without a named decision-maker and deadline is information, not control. Someone must have the authority to accept the exposure, fund the response or explain why another course is justified. Following the process is important, although it's not the same as preventing the loss. Insurance can help change the economics of prevention Insurers can make recommendations easier to act on by explaining the severity and urgency of an exposure, not simply recording that it exists. Brokers can connect risk-engineering findings with an organization's insurance and resilience priorities. Operators must determine whether to intervene or accept the exposure and take responsibility for the outcome. There is also a bigger opportunity here. Insurers and brokers possess extraordinary expertise in understanding, quantifying, and pricing risk. Much of that expertise has historically helped organizations prepare financially for potential losses. What if more of it could be applied to making prevention economically compelling before those losses occur? Imagine insurers, brokers, and industrial operators working from a more continuous, consequence-based understanding of emerging physical risk. Rather than relying primarily on historical losses and periodic assessments, they could better understand where exposure is developing, which conditions present the greatest business consequences, and where intervention could materially reduce risk. This wouldn't eliminate uncertainty or diminish the need for insurance. It could, however, create a stronger economic foundation for prevention and a more productive relationship between risk financing and operational decision-making. For decades, the insurance industry has helped businesses understand the financial consequences of what can go wrong. That expertise will remain indispensable, but the next opportunity is to help make the economics of what doesn't have to go wrong equally visible. We've become extraordinarily good at financing industrial failure. It's time to become just as disciplined about investing in its prevention. items.summary: Why Can't We Fund Prevention? items.rss_description: November 2026 ITL FOCUS: Pricing & Rating RyanMeyer Mon, 11/02/2026 - 12:00 ITL FOCUS is a monthly initiative featuring topics related to innovation in risk management and insurance. November 2, 2026 FROM THE EDITOR Pricing is one of the most consequential functions in insurance — and one of the least visible. Claims gets the headlines. Underwriting gets the scrutiny. But pricing sits quietly underneath both, shaping profitability across millions of policies through assumptions that can go stale faster than anyone realizes. For most carriers, the mechanics of pricing haven’t kept pace with how quickly the world is changing. A rate change approved today might not be live in the market for weeks or months, trapped behind policy administration release cycles that were never designed for the kind of volatility the industry is now dealing with — social inflation, rising repair costs, tariff pressure, and catastrophe losses that keep defying historical patterns. Kumarappan Sundaram has spent years working through these problems with P&C carriers as a Managing Director at PwC. He brings a technology practitioner’s perspective to a function that often gets treated as a back-office infrastructure problem rather than a strategic capability. He’s measured about where AI fits — distinguishing what is already delivering clear value from what remains genuinely unproven — and direct about the sequencing mistakes carriers make when they try to modernize pricing before the foundation is in place. His practical advice is worth taking seriously: Before reaching for advanced analytics or AI, measure how long it actually takes to get an approved rate change into the market. Most carriers have never done that math. The number, he suggests, tends to be illuminating. Read the full interview to find out why decoupling rating logic from the core policy system is the starting point most carriers skip, how modern pricing platforms are beginning to close the long-standing gap between pricing and underwriting, and where AI can genuinely change the work. Pricing at the Speed of the Market Paul Carroll, Editor-in-chief of Insurance Thought Leadership. Pricing gets far less attention than claims or underwriting, yet it is important. How is the pricing function being modernized in insurance? And how should it be? Kumarappan Sundaram, Managing Director, PwC US Pricing gets less attention partly because a lot of the work is infrastructure: platforms, data flows and deployment processes. It is not a front-office workflow that a new tool can visibly transform. Modernization can be uneven. Personal lines are well on their way. Commercial lines are earlier in the journey and still rely heavily on underwriter judgment and rating engines embedded in policy administration systems. How pricing should be modernized can largely be a question of sequence. The foundation comes first: decoupling rating from the policy admin system. At the moment, actuaries produce pricing logic, which they hand to IT, which embeds the logic in a rating engine that sits within a policy admin system. So, making a change to the pricing logic means waiting for a new release of the policy admin system. If you decouple, you can make changes to ratings as and when you want. Once you’ve decoupled, you should build reliable data flows and establish clear governance. You can then go to the next level of capabilities, like advanced analytics and AI. Let’s say you have a $10 billion book. You’re considering changing a particular rate factor from X to Y, maybe related to driver age. Advanced analytics can help you understand the impact of the rate change on the whole book. The actuaries can then decide whether to make that rate change. Carriers can help deploy and monitor pricing changes quickly and safely. Paul Carroll From a technology standpoint, what are the most important shifts in P&C pricing and rating? Read More Breaking Down Silos in Insurance by Rory Meleniclis Insurers can dismantle organizational silos by shifting from project-based work to product teams built around shared capabilities like underwriting and claims. Read More How AI Can Transform Submissions for Underwriting by Prathap Gokul Commercial insurers face a strategic challenge: identifying which submissions merit scarce underwriting attention, not just processing more faster. items.title: Insurers Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.original_title: Insurers Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.rss_title: Insurers Fraud Targets Seniors Online
items.rss_description: Insurers Fraud Targets Seniors Online Life & Health ITL Editorial Team Wed, 11/04/2026 - 13:16 Scammers increasingly impersonate insurers to steal identities and money during open enrollment. November 12, 2026 Image Last year, the Justice Department brought the largest healthcare fraud case in its history, which included charges that criminals stole the identities of more than 1 million Americans to submit $10.6 billion in fraudulent Medicare claims for urinary catheters. While Medicare blocked nearly all of it, private Medicare supplemental insurers paid out about $900 million. Americans lost a record $20.9 billion to internet crime in 2025, up 26% in one year, according to the FBI. Insurance fraud, including healthcare fraud, costs Americans more than $300 billion a year, and health insurance scams pick up during open enrollment, the FTC says. Seniors are the hardest-hit age group, losing $7.7 billion in 2025, up 59% in one year. In fact, Michigan officials warned on Oct. 12 of impostors claiming to be from Medicare to dupe older adults. As co-founder of Spokeo , a people search company, and former co-chair of the W3C Credentials Community Group , I have witnessed firsthand how scammers have grown increasingly sophisticated over the last 20 years. Insurance scams are evolving and costly We are seeing many insurance-related scams in 2026. Fraudsters are buying sponsored search ads with web addresses and logos that look very similar to HealthCare.gov and Medicare.gov . When Americans click on the link, they end up buying a plan that is not real insurance and also fork over their personal information, which can lead to identity theft. Even large health insurers are being duped, as the $900 million loss in the catheter case shows. items.extracted_text: Cortina: Just a soft market trend, or clearing the floor for reinsurance's next act? - Artemis.bm Cortina: Just a soft market trend, or clearing the floor for reinsurance's next act? - Artemis.bm Cortina: Just a soft market trend, or clearing the floor for reinsurance’s next act? 13th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Cortina has raised a lot of questions in the market, as to whether the recently launched Aon structured and Blackstone backed reinsurance facility at Lloyd’s is simply the latest iteration of a soft market trend and evolution of following, tracker style capacity, or something more portending of future market developments. There’s a fascinating metaphor buried in the name Cortina, one that we completely missed. Kudos to the analyst team at J.P. Morgan led by Kamran Hossain for spotting it, bringing it to our attention in their latest report and providing the inspiration. A Cortina is a specific tango-related phrase, a brief musical interlude within the Argentine milonga (a social tango event), used to signal the end of one dance, the clearing of the floor for a new set of dancers, and it often signals a structural change to the rhythm that has been played. Apply that to reinsurance and the Lloyd’s market and Cortina becomes a signal of something potentially more meaningful and perhaps ominous, than just an extension of Aon’s Client Treaty with a single backer. The use of lead-follow capacity strategies at Lloyd’s is not new, in fact the market has been dancing to the same rhythm for decades. This has relied on a deep network of pure-play reinsurers, falling into line behind a lead underwriter. While the recent launch of Cortina syndicate 1956 gave little away in terms of the thinking behind the structure or strategy, aside from it being a way for Blackstone ( third-party capital ) to secure preferential access to a large amount of reinsurance business from Lloyd’s, and for Aon to better serve its clients with capacity, the applicability of this tango-related metaphor is perhaps striking. Cortina could act as the market’s musical break, signalling a fundamental and maybe structural shift in who provides follow capacity and on what terms. Introducing a dynamic that may play out across the risk transfer ecosystem (much more broadly than within the Lloyd’s market alone) with ramifications for incumbents across reinsurance. Going back to the metaphor, in tango the Cortina is when the musical lead orchestrates the dance, cuing up a new rhythm or genre and structurally changing the flow of the evening. In reinsurance, the broker’s are increasingly orchestrating the flow of capital and how it gets matched with risk. By arranging a facility like Cortina, which has the ability to automatically write 3% of eligible property catastrophe excess-of-loss treaties and 5% of other eligible treaties arranged by Aon, the broker is actively curating the flow of premium to meet the needs of large capital providers. Aon is routing efficient, lower-friction institutional capital increasingly directly to the risk, bypassing the more traditional open-market syndication. If the Cortina strategy delivers for all parties, returning structural savings to cedants as a dividend-style discount to lead terms, delivering returns to the investors and importantly adding value for the brokers, then we can expect more of these structures to be cued up. Back to the metaphor. You could say that, the brokers are dictating the playlist and adjusting the rhythm of the reinsurance market, and alternative capital is increasingly their preferred track. Sticking with the tango, when the Cortina gets played it also signals a separation of the previous sets of partners. In follow-form facilities and broker facilities, traditional reinsurers and syndicates have often relied on the flow of premiums they deliver, as passive and often lucrative access to flow business can be a meaningful addition to their own underwriting efforts. With the use of the Lloyd’s infrastructure, alongside insurance-linked securities market plumbing in the form of the London Bridge 2 structure, initiatives like Cortina could bring in institutional and private credit-like asset management giants in the place of the more traditional capacity partner. Returning to the tango metaphor again, through Cortina, Blackstone can channel capital onto the dance floor without the operational friction, legacy liabilities, or high expense ratios associated with building a standalone reinsurance franchise. They are not there to debate the steps, they are there to execute their strategy (dance) algorithmically, strictly following the lead underwriter’s terms and claims decisions. This represents a further commoditisation of follow capacity by the ILS and alternative capital markets, although it also has broader ramifications outside pure follow-form strategies. When the Cortina plays in an Argentinian dancehall, it never signals the end of the night, but it does signal a changing, or mixing of the dance floor’s participants and fundamentally, sometimes structurally, resets the room. There are potentially significant implications of course, for those operating within Lloyd’s and perhaps beyond. The strategy has implications for anyone relying on follow-form access to premiums, especially syndicates that lack the specialist expertise to consistently lead complex placements in the underwriting market. Access to risk could be reduced, while the ability of the broker’s to reliably fill large amounts of a slip with efficient institutional capital could reduce some market participants pricing power and relevance. Those with the capability to price and lead on underwriting, while setting the terms and managing the claims in the process as well, may be able to command a premium, which does have the potential to bifurcate the market to a degree. Back to our tango metaphor, incumbents will need to be able to justify their expense ratios through top-tier underwriting talent and proprietary data, as those that are unable to lead the dance may struggle to secure their spot on the floor. Efficient following capacity at scale from players with potentially lower costs-of-capital also introduces a new pricing dynamic into the reinsurance market. Over-time, developments like this that become more widespread have the potential to compress pricing, make premium harder to come by and force incumbent reinsurers to compress their own margins to compete with the efficiency of institutional capital deployed through low-friction vehicles that borrow techniques from the insurance-linked securities market structure and form. Follow capacity, so-called ReShares and now increasingly we hear people in the market talking about indexing to meet large investors appetite. The broker that enables investors to access index-like returns more efficiently in reinsurance stands to gain a lot of power, which makes it a prize worth pursuing and this is starting to generate real attention it seems. It’s unclear at this stage whether Cortina is simply the latest remix of an old and established dance tune, or something more radical and heralding of real change, in the rhythm and flow of the reinsurance market. As broker’s own analytics, data, technology and pricing capabilities accelerate and become increasingly powerful in their own right, it does also raise questions over who is actually leading the dance these days and will be in future? Cortina syndicate 1956 sends yet another clear signal that the convergence of alternative, institutional capital and traditional reinsurance continues to evolve beyond the typical ILS structures we’ve seen for years and now occupies a growing role in the everyday flow of syndicated placements as well. For the traditional market, Cortina signals it. The music has changed and it’s time to learn the correct steps for a new rhythm that is being played. items.title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.original_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_title: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop'
items.rss_description: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop' PaulCarroll Tue, 11/10/2026 - 12:55 The notion that there must always be a "human in the loop" has become de rigueur in any discussion of AI implementation in business. The cynical side of me suspects that part of the reason is to reassure everyone that AI won't lead to mass layoffs, but there are also plenty of practical reasons to have humans check the work of AIs. Or maybe not. At least not for long. A recent article in Harvard Business Review argues that human supervisors quickly become numb and simply approve the recommendations of the AI as it becomes increasingly accurate. And I think the author has a point, based on what I've seen of human/AI interactions in semi-autonomous cars. There needs to be a better way. Let's have a look. Early in the development of its driverless cars, Google gave demo models to employees. Google warned them that the AI wasn't perfect and instructed them to have their hands on the wheel, always ready to take control. That worked... for a little while. A very little while. As the AI proved to be reliable, the drivers began to relax their hold on the wheel, then started to take their eyes off the road, then began reading or looking at their phones. When the car signaled that the drivers had to take over, they needed perhaps 10 seconds to fully reengage. Given that a car going 60mph travels nearly 300 yards in 10 seconds, Google realized its hybrid approach wouldn't work and committed to producing only cars that could be fully autonomous. Other makers of autonomous vehicles, most notably Tesla, continue to offer cars that take a hybrid, human/AI approach, but I think that's irresponsible (as I wrote at length a year ago). Now, an article in Harvard Business Review offers a similar view about the dangers of having a "human in the loop" to supervise work done by AIs. The author, a senior fellow at Cal, writes: "Decades of research on automation show that better automation systems lead to worse human safety layers; as automation grows more reliable, the people monitoring it grow complacent, their skills atrophy, and they become less attentive.... AI compounds the problem. Its failures sound as confident, fluent, and well-structured as its successes.... "Even when validation works and people catch errors, every correction is captured as training data. Each exception a person handles teaches the system to handle that exception; the better the data, the smaller the scope of human validation needed in the future." The article says the lack of reliability of the humans in the loop is actually just the start of the problem. He writes: "The larger problem with the human-in-the-loop organization, though, is that the entire blueprint reads the transformation backwards. It organizes the company around the shrinking frontier of what machines can’t yet do. But there’s a larger opportunity here. Because AI removes constraints, it enables new combinations of work, new decision rights, and new forms of value. Organizations, accordingly, have an opportunity to reorganize and 'rebundle' around those new decisions rather than the shrinking residue of the old work." He goes on to lay out how to think about rebundling: "Instead of asking which tasks the machine can take over, leading organizations should ask which new roles the technology makes possible, and then redesign the organization around them." He lists several steps that can lead you to new approaches, which seem intriguing and which you may want to explore. For now, though, I just want to make the point that "human in the loop" isn't a panacea, certainly not in the long term. The reviewers of AI work can quickly become as reliant on the AI as those Google employees who found themselves with their hands off the wheel, their eyes off the road and their minds far away from driving when a problem popped up in front of them. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll An HBR article argues that human supervisors quickly become unreliable as the AI becomes increasingly accurate. items.summary: The Flaw in 'Human-in-the-Loop' PaulCarroll Tue, 11/10/2026 - 12:55 The notion that there must always be a "human in the loop" has become de rigueur in any discussion of AI implementation in business. The cynical side of me suspects that part of the reason is to reassure everyone that AI won't lead to mass layoffs, but there are also plenty of practical reasons to have humans check the work of AIs. Or maybe not. At least not for long. A recent article in Harvard Business Review argues that human supervisors quickly become numb and simply approve the recommendations of the AI as it becomes increasingly accurate. And I think the author has a point, based on what I've seen of human/AI interactions in semi-autonomous cars. There needs to be a better way. Let's have a look. Early in the development of its driverless cars, Google gave demo models to employees. Google warned them that the AI wasn't perfect and instructed them to have their hands on the wheel, always ready to take control. That worked... for a little while. A very little while. As the AI proved to be reliable, the drivers began to relax their hold on the wheel, then started to take their eyes off the road, then began reading or looking at their phones. When the car signaled that the drivers had to take over, they needed perhaps 10 seconds to fully reengage. Given that a car going 60mph travels nearly 300 yards in 10 seconds, Google realized its hybrid approach wouldn't work and committed to producing only cars that could be fully autonomous. Other makers of autonomous vehicles, most notably Tesla, continue to offer cars that take a hybrid, human/AI approach, but I think that's irresponsible (as I wrote at length a year ago). Now, an article in Harvard Business Review offers a similar view about the dangers of having a "human in the loop" to supervise work done by AIs. The author, a senior fellow at Cal, writes: "Decades of research on automation show that better automation systems lead to worse human safety layers; as automation grows more reliable, the people monitoring it grow complacent, their skills atrophy, and they become less attentive.... AI compounds the problem. Its failures sound as confident, fluent, and well-structured as its successes.... "Even when validation works and people catch errors, every correction is captured as training data. Each exception a person handles teaches the system to handle that exception; the better the data, the smaller the scope of human validation needed in the future." The article says the lack of reliability of the humans in the loop is actually just the start of the problem. He writes: "The larger problem with the human-in-the-loop organization, though, is that the entire blueprint reads the transformation backwards. It organizes the company around the shrinking frontier of what machines can’t yet do. But there’s a larger opportunity here. Because AI removes constraints, it enables new combinations of work, new decision rights, and new forms of value. Organizations, accordingly, have an opportunity to reorganize and 'rebundle' around those new decisions rather than the shrinking residue of the old work." He goes on to lay out how to think about rebundling: "Instead of asking which tasks the machine can take over, leading organizations should ask which new roles the technology makes possible, and then redesign the organization around them." He lists several steps that can lead you to new approaches, which seem intriguing and which you may want to explore. For now, though, I just want to make the point that "human in the loop" isn't a panacea, certainly not in the long term. The reviewers of AI work can quickly become as reliant on the AI as those Google employees who found themselves with their hands off the wheel, their eyes off the road and their minds far away from driving when a problem popped up in front of them. Cheers, Paul Image Paul Carroll An HBR article argues that human supervisors quickly become unreliable as the AI becomes increasingly accurate. items.extracted_text: Hours-Long Microsoft Outage Disrupts Businesses, Governments Globally Article 0 Comments A more than 12-hour outage of Microsoft Outlook and Teams crippled communications for businesses and governments globally on Friday, forcing some organizations to revert to fax machines and halting at least one bond repurchase in Europe. Microsoft said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant and that a broader roll-out of software fixes was starting to stabilize the system. It said it was not aware of any malicious activity. Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings. Read more: Microsoft Races to Fix Outlook in One of Its Longest Outages It affected government agencies from Australia to Japan and the United States, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements. Organizations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared. Another Outage for Microsoft The outage is one of the longest in Microsoft’s history and the second disruption to its services this year. Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online – its cloud-based email and scheduling hub – leaving unconnected applications operational. The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it. Microsoft shares fell 1.7% before the bell, lagging the broader market. They have gained roughly 8% so far this year. “The bigger worry is that this is not the first Microsoft 365 outage this year,” said Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at trading platform eToro. “If reliability starts to look like a recurring problem, it hands every IT department a reason to think twice before putting even more of their business in one provider’s hands.” Still, some analysts have questioned whether such incidents can push customers on to rivals due to the steep switching costs of replacing tools embedded so deeply in daily operations. Microsoft faced an outage with its 365 services in January this year and also in October last year. Last month, it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software, and a range of industries worldwide. Trades Had to Be Confirmed by Fax A spokesperson for the UK government said it was working with Microsoft to find a solution for the outage that hit organizations such as the NHS and London’s Metropolitan Police. Lack of access emails and other services was impacting the Metropolitan Police’s ability to report some crimes online, though its ability to respond to calls was not affected. NHS said its local services were turning to alternate measures such as using IT systems or paper records. For businesses, the fallout was widespread. European exchange operator Euronext reported email disruptions, British insurer Aviva activated backups for its earnings calls and Danish shipping giant Maersk warned customers of delayed updates. American AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic also faced issues with Microsoft connectors, while Indian airlines IndiGo, Akasa Air and Air India said their email support services were impacted. The outage also disrupted fund management at Taiwanese securities firms, life insurers, and investment trust companies. One of the companies went as far as canceling a bond repurchase transaction, a source familiar with the situation told Reuters. Another Taiwanese financial company resorted to using fax to confirm trades, a second source said. In the US, electric truck maker Workhorse Group rescheduled its results on Thursday to November 16, while Switzerland’s Richemont briefly delayed its first-half results announcement on Friday. In Australia, where the spy agency and federal police were among organizations caught in the outage, Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said Microsoft does not suspect a cyber attack. “The impact that they are dealing with … is very much on email systems,” the minister added. (Reporting by Aditya Soni, Harshita Mary Varghese, Anzar Mehraj, Katha Kalia, Preetika Parashuraman, Shubham Kalia, and Akanksha Khushi in Bengaluru, Stefica Bikesh in Sydney, Chris Thomas and Mrinmay Dey in Mexico City, Liang-sa Loh in Taipei additional reporting by Jeffrey Dastin editing by Leroy Leo, Stephen Coates, Elaine Hardcastle, Devika Syamnath) Copyright 2026 Reuters. items.title: Viewpoint: The Cyber Insurance Industry’s AI Blind Spot
items.original_title: Viewpoint: The Cyber Insurance Industry’s AI Blind Spot
items.rss_title: Viewpoint: The Cyber Insurance Industry’s AI Blind Spot
items.rss_description: Highly sophisticated AI tools have become integral to modern business operations. According to McKinsey & Company, 88% of organizations report regular AI use in at least one business function. But as businesses adopt AI, the insurance market is still playing …
items.extracted_text: Viewpoint: The Cyber Insurance Industry’s AI Blind Spot Article 0 Comments Highly sophisticated AI tools have become integral to modern business operations. According to McKinsey & Company, 88% of organizations report regular AI use in at least one business function. But as businesses adopt AI, the insurance market is still playing catch-up when it contributes to a loss. The broader the adoption of AI, the greater the concern about how malicious actors can weaponize AI against businesses. In response, many carriers are choosing paths that prioritize their own risk avoidance over the survival of their policyholders. This primarily takes two forms in the market: blanket AI exclusions or complete silence in policy language. Both approaches can undermine the value of cyber insurance for policyholders and create uncertainty across the wider industry. Retreat leaves policyholders scrambling In the last few years, nearly 83% of the S&P 500 flagged AI as a material risk and 87% of executives identified AI-related vulnerabilities as the fastest-growing cyber risk. Yet, more than 60 P/C insurance groups filed to adopt AI exclusions. While not all those organizations have implemented them, their filings are a clear signal of the industry’s nervousness toward AI-related risks — even though AI has become a critical business tool and an increasingly important part of the cyber risk landscape. Depending on the wording, a broad AI exclusion will enable a carrier to challenge or deny a claim simply because an AI tool was involved, even if human error — which a typical cyber insurance policy covers — primarily drove the loss. Even if an insurer clarifies the difference between AI-related security incidents and others, it can still diminish the value of coverage by weakening policyholders’ confidence that their coverage will respond when needed. In a world where most modern software stacks now integrate AI, an absolute exclusion signals an inability to adapt underwriting and risk models to emerging risks. This incongruence can create coverage gaps, leaving policyholders even more exposed. Silence begets policyholder confusion Another tactic employed by insurers is the wait-and-see approach: they remain silent on AI and avoid any mention in their policy wording altogether. This omission doesn’t mean no response to an AI-related exposure, but vague language leaves coverage open to interpretation, which creates headaches for both the insurer and the insured. In the event of a coverage dispute, businesses may face the cost and uncertainty of a legal battle simply to determine whether their insurance safety net exists. Carriers also take on unintended risk when policy language does not clearly address how AI-related events will be treated. Without clear, affirmative wording, traditional cyber coverage may create uncertainty when an AI model is involved in a security failure or privacy breach, leaving organizations with silent AI exposures. What the market needs Much of the insurance market is treating AI as a terrifying, unquantifiable specter when it is really an accelerated evolution of the digital threats the industry has managed for decades. Most AI-driven incidents do not represent entirely new cyber risks they’re familiar threats powered or enhanced by new technology. Take business email compromise, for example, where bad actors trick victims into sending money or private data by pretending to be trusted associates. The FBI has been tracking this exposure since the early 2010s . It remains the most common event type, representing 31% of all claims in 2025. With AI, bad actors can now amass even more information about their targets during the reconnaissance stage to spoof email addresses, hyper-personalize messages, translate their messages into different languages, and boost their success rate. The underlying exposure remains the same, but AI has made these attack methods more effective. The same logic applies to deepfake-enabled fraud. An employee who sends funds after receiving an AI-generated voice message impersonating a CFO has suffered a familiar funds transfer fraud loss. The delivery mechanism has changed, but the underlying business impact has not. Leveraging AI for better cyber defense Conversely, defenders can use AI to defend against attacks and potentially reduce losses. Many managed detection and response (MDR) platforms use automation and AI-assisted triage to evaluate alerts rapidly, helping security teams identify and respond to fast-moving threats. MDR is a key part of protecting an organization against fast-moving cyber threats. Many leading MDR tools use AI to automatically triage threat detections in milliseconds. MDR is a scalable, cost-effective service that can shield businesses from advanced cyber risks more effectively than traditional risk management tools and offerings. That reinforces the broader point: AI should be evaluated as part of the overall risk environment, not treated as an automatic reason to exclude coverage. The industry has the data, security tools, and underwriting capabilities needed to accurately price and evaluate cyber risk in the age of AI, so it has no excuse for defaulting to broad exclusions or, worse, silence. Instead, carriers should pursue affirmative policy language that explicitly states how coverage responds to AI-driven threats. The industry needs cyber policies designed to evolve with the risk landscape and respond to the outcome of the incident, not the technology behind it. Whether an exposure originates with a human or an AI model, the consequences are real, and the cyber insurance market should be able to absorb them. As new risks arise, it’s crucial for businesses to feel confident that they have a partner who can help them recover from a damaging incident. Anything short of that is a market failure. items.extracted_text: Cat bond market breadth expands, issuance concentrates in 1% to 3% EL range: Euler ILS Partners - Artemis.bm Cat bond market breadth expands, issuance concentrates in 1% to 3% EL range: Euler ILS Partners - Artemis.bm Cat bond market breadth expands, issuance concentrates in 1% to 3% EL range: Euler ILS Partners 12th November 2026 - Author: Steve Evans Through the recent period of brisk issuance the catastrophe bond market has been expanding rapidly, with now 20% more cat bond deals available to investors than a year ago, analysis from specialist Swiss insurance-linked securities investment manager Euler ILS Partners shows. In its review of the market after the third-quarter of 2026, Euler ILS Partners found that the size of the market had increased 17.3% year-on-year, while the number of deals outstanding rose slightly faster by 20% to reach 402. This expansion in market breadth means more individual investment opportunities are available to cat bond fund managers and investors, which helps in portfolio construction and diversification. But the metrics speak to a softening marketplace, with the average coupon of the cat bond market down 9.2% at 7.14% and the average spread down faster with a 21.6% decline YoY to 5.05%. The market has seen its issuance increasingly concentrated in the 1% to 3% expected loss range, Euler ILS Partners noted, which has raised the average expected loss of outstanding catastrophe bonds by 12.5% YoY to 2.4%. Euler ILS Partners’ data previously showed the average expected loss of the cat bond market had risen from 2.29% at the end of Q1 2026 to 2.31% by the end of the second-quarter , so the increase has continued. Euler ILS Partners commented as to how the market’s expected loss has developed, saying, “The share of issuance in the 1% to 3% expected-loss range increased from 37% in 2018 to 64% in 2026 YTD. As a result, lower-EL layers have become less prevalent in new issuance.” You can see how expected losses of catastrophe bond issuance have developed by year in the chart below, which shows the weighted average across 2026 issuance so far at 2.67%. Unweighted, Artemis’ data on catastrophe bond issuance expected losses shows the average at 2.85% in 2026 to-date, which is now the highest level since 2019 . Euler ILS Partners chart (above) shows issuance contracting fastest in the 1% to 2% EL range and increasing in the 2% to 3% range, which suggests the weighted average may increase further as this year progresses. Through reinsurance market cycles the average expected loss of cat bond issuance tends to rise when prices soften, as sponsors capitalise on being able to bring higher-risk deals to market. At the same time, through the third-quarter of 2026 the composition of perils in the cat bond market remained relatively stable according to Euler ILS Partners’ data. items.rss_description: A group of nonprofits sued OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX’s AI division, Meta Platforms and Alphabet’s Google on Thursday, seeking to block the further development of the most advanced AI models over concerns, voiced by the companies’ own leaders, that the technology …
items.extracted_text: OpenAI, Google, Anthropic Hit With Lawsuit Seeking Halt to Frontier AI Development Article 0 Comments A group of nonprofits sued OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX’s AI division, Meta Platforms and Alphabet’s Google on Thursday, seeking to block the further development of the most advanced AI models over concerns, voiced by the companies’ own leaders, that the technology could pose a threat to humanity. The nonprofits, which focus on tech accountability and include the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen and Heat Initiative, sued in San Francisco, saying California’s laws against unfair business practices provide the grounds for a court order barring the companies from further development of products like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude. The lawsuit cites comments from company leaders, like Dario Amodei, chief executive of Anthropic, and Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive, about AI’s potential to cause the destruction of civilization. It also describes recent incidents where models have escaped testing environments and autonomously attacked government websites. “No other industry is allowed to treat its own development of unsafe products—much less ones that could kill us all—as inevitable,” the lawsuit says. “Nor is any industry granted the right to self-regulate the development of such dangerous products.” The lawsuit accuses the companies of engaging in business practices that create a public nuisance, or harm to public health and enjoyment, pointing to both past incidents and the potential for future harm. A spokesperson for Meta declined to comment. Representatives of the other companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Other Lawsuits Seek to Bar Development While the Trump administration has so far declined to pursue large-scale AI regulation over fears it could harm the country’s ability to compete with China, states and private entities have sought to use lawsuits to force the companies to make changes. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier sued OpenAI in June, accusing the company of misrepresenting the safety of its ChatGPT platform, saying it has harmed children by providing information to school shooters, offering guidance on self-harm and addicting young users. In September, Florida asked the judge overseeing the lawsuit to bar OpenAI from developing new artificial intelligence models without outside oversight. That motion remains pending, according to court records. After Florida’s filing, OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the company had paused training its most capable models and would not resume until they have additional safeguards in place. “Governments have an important role to play in setting robust safety standards for AI, and we’re committed to working with Florida and other states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry – not just one company,” Pusateri said. Separately, a group of eight states sued OpenAI last month in courts across the country alleging ChatGPT has coached its users — including teenagers — to harm themselves or others. OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment after the filing. The states’ lawsuits seek financial penalties, as well as an order barring the company ⁠from developing self-improving AI models unless it can ensure those models are aligned with human values. items.title: White Workers Claiming Discrimination Complicates Shell’s DEI Drive
items.original_title: White Workers Claiming Discrimination Complicates Shell’s DEI Drive
items.rss_title: White Workers Claiming Discrimination Complicates Shell’s DEI Drive
items.rss_description: In October, Shell Plc held a “DE&I in Action and World Mental Health” day, focused on inclusion and mental wellbeing. Staff in the U.S. and elsewhere were encouraged to reflect on their experiences at work, to “practice care, courage and …
items.extracted_text: White Workers Claiming Discrimination Complicates Shell’s DEI Drive Article 0 Comments In October, Shell Plc held a “DE&I in Action and World Mental Health” day, focused on inclusion and mental wellbeing. Staff in the U.S. and elsewhere were encouraged to reflect on their experiences at work, to “practice care, courage and curiosity” and to use a special video-conference background to mark the occasion. For an oil major that does business with the U.S. government, the mere existence of the event is notable. At a time when many global companies are downplaying diversity measures, London-headquartered Shell — which counts the U.S. as its biggest country market — is vocal in its commitment to diversity, equity and inclusion, calling it “a key driver for our winning performance culture.” That stance helps Shell comply with global diversity regulations that are non-negotiable for businesses based outside of the U.S. But it also increases the risk of scrutiny from the Trump administration and conservative activists. Shell’s DEI commitment has become central to legal challenges filed by three current or former employees represented by an activist group co-founded by President Donald Trump’s new Chief of Staff, Stephen Miller. The workers claim to have been discriminated against because they are White, describing a team restructure that favored ethnic-minority colleagues and foreign nationals, as well as a manager who they say gave them “tear jars” as jokey leaving gifts, which they found insensitive. The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — whose Trump-appointed chair has urged White men to report workplace discrimination — did not take up the case but gave the trio notice of the right to sue, an administrative step. In March, a judge will review whether one of the cases is ready to proceed to trial, according to court filings. Stephen Miller Photographer: Bonnie Cash/UPI/Bloomberg Shell strongly rebuts the allegations, a company spokesperson said, adding that it does not tolerate discrimination and makes employment decisions based on merit and business needs. The business complies with local laws and regulations in countries where it operates, the spokesperson added. Shell also said in a legal filing that the unit the plaintiffs worked for has a long-standing practice of giving departing employees iconic blue-and-white Dutch pottery in recognition of their time at the company. Employment discrimination lawsuits don’t typically threaten large corporations’ core operations or business viability. And people with knowledge of the oil and gas sector said that firms like Shell broadly have good relationships with the Trump administration and more pressing concerns than DEI. Nonetheless, these cases can cause reputational damage, incur legal costs and soak up managers’ time and attention. They also show how Trump’s DEI pushback is being pursued. “We’re seeing more enforcement activity where we hadn’t seen enforcement activity before,” said Samia Kirmani, a Boston-based attorney at Jackson Lewis PC, which focuses on employment law. The EEOC has already stepped up its pursuit of DEI-related cases through policy statements and guidance notified Fortune 500 companies that it’s prepared to litigate over DEI filed a lawsuit against a Coca-Cola Co. distributor over a women’s-only retreat and this month settled with Lockheed Martin Corp. over alleged discrimination against White employees related to performance and compensation decisions. While the Democrats’ landslide victory in the midterm elections this month has altered the political landscape, the implications for government actions on DEI remain to be seen. Of the 32 workplace DEI-discrimination lawsuits ongoing across the country right now, most concern White people claiming discrimination, according to New York University’s Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion and Belonging. In addition to the EEOC’s growing appetite for enforcement, there are President Trump’s own executive orders and directives from the Department of Justice to consider, Kirmani said, meaning businesses across the board can’t ignore the prospect of future legal action. Scaling Back In the American workforce, White people hold about 80% of all management roles and have one of the lowest unemployment rates of any cohort. The Trump administration has prioritized fighting what it describes as racism against White workers, barring federal contractors from engaging in “illegal DEI.” In response, companies like McDonald’s Corp. and Ford Motor Co. have scaled back their inclusion efforts. Meanwhile, Shell, which is among the world’s largest energy companies and is enjoying healthy financial growth after several years of cost-cutting, has continued to set measurable global diversity targets, although it does not target specific numbers in the U.S. It aims for women to hold 40% of global senior leadership positions by 2030. It maintains a Global Council for Race — a group of senior Shell leaders aiming to advance workforce diversity, who do not make individual employment decisions — and supports employee groups focused on race and ethnicity, as well as LGBTQ+ and disability inclusion. In the U.K. and European Union, where diversity rules mainly focus on gender rather than race, companies are required to meet targets and follow disclosure rules around things like board diversity, gender pay gaps and pay transparency. Countries including Japan and Australia also impose diversity regulations on corporations. To operate in these jurisdictions, U.S. companies must meet these requirements too, regardless of their approach at home. Thomas Hutt holds the tear jar he says was given to him by his former boss at Shell. Photographer: Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg Measures like holding DEI events aren’t specifically covered by these regulations. But the oil and gas industry often struggles to bring in women and needs to maintain a balanced global workforce to do business in many countries, said Alison Taylor, a clinical associate professor at New York University who focuses on corporate responsibility and business ethics. “They tend to operate via moving people around,” she said. In lawsuits filed in Texas, the most recent of them in August, three people who work or have worked in Shell’s U.S. corporate security unit allege that the company violated employment laws. They are seeking back pay, compensation for future lost earnings, benefits and damages from Shell, without specifying a figure. The plaintiffs allege that the oil company favored minority workers at their expense during a restructuring of their division in January 2025 — just as Trump was beginning his second term and when many companies were already scaling back their DEI efforts. Miller’s America First Legal, which lists dismantling DEI as a priority on its website, is also representing White people in cases against corporations including TV network CBS, Meta Platforms Inc. and International Business Machines Corp. “Federal civil rights laws protect every American, and America First Legal is fighting to hold Shell accountable for violating those protections in the name of ‘DEI,'” AFL spokeswoman Alexa Vance said in an emailed statement. “Shell touts its commitment to ‘diversity’ while simultaneously showing high-performing, longtime employees the door because they are White.” Complaints like those against Shell are victories for right-wing groups because they support their broader media campaign and narrative, said Jonathan Feingold, a law professor at Boston University. “Large corporations often have actually pretty shallow commitments to reckon with the way in which misogyny or racism manifest in their institutions,” he said. In his complaint, Thomas Hutt, a former manager in Shell’s corporate security unit, said he was forced to reapply for his role after almost 15 years at the company, during which he received strong performance reviews. Hutt said his manager Wayne Hunt, a defendant in the case, had said he was looking to “diversify the talent.” Hutt said he was ultimately replaced by a Black colleague who, in his view, lacked experience in corporate security, having previously worked in fraud investigations. When he left the job, Hutt said that Hunt gave him a “tear jar” — a small, decorative vessel, supposedly for collecting tears — to mock him. Two of Hutt’s colleagues, Kevin Taylor and Michelle Romak, jointly filed a similar complaint in August last year. They said they were told to reapply for their roles during the 2025 reorganization, while minority employees weren’t. They allege that some minority applicants for jobs within the team got preferential treatment, such as interview coaching. In a formal written response to the allegations dated Oct. 16, 2025, Shell said that a coaching session was to help an employee join its corporate security group, not to prepare them for interviews. Taylor, who still works at Shell, said in the complaint that he was demoted and forced to transfer from company headquarters to another state, while a Hispanic contractor, who Taylor said was under-performing, was given his preferred role. In its response, Shell denied the allegations but accepted that Hunt had approved Taylor’s transfer. Romak was ultimately laid off and said Hunt also gave her a tear jar. The EEOC declined to comment, while the White House didn’t respond to emails seeking comment. Polarized Views During an internal company webcast around the time of Trump’s January 2025 inauguration, Shell Chief Legal Officer Philippa Bounds was asked how Trump’s policies may affect its contracts and said the company was not turning its back on DEI, according to a former employee who declined to be identified discussing internal communications. Shell did not comment on the matter. On employee-review website Glassdoor, Shell ranks 4.1 out of 5 for its DE&I measures. Some employees have also praised the company’s efforts on platforms like LinkedIn, where one employee wrote earlier this year that she was proud to work with “everyone who makes diversity, equity and inclusion real.” But for some former employees in the U.S., Shell’s approach has been a frustration. One ex-supervisor who worked offshore said he believed staff reductions disproportionately affected White, male workers and that he was compelled to give presentations on LGBTQ issues that he felt conflicted with his Christian faith. The supervisor declined to be identified, citing a non-disclosure agreement. Another former offshore worker, who also asked not to be named, said he believed Shell aimed to make its Whale production platform the most diverse in the Gulf of Mexico and that managers actively sought Black and other minority employees for leadership-development programs. In his view, DEI impacted morale among White, male employees who felt overlooked and unable to voice criticism. As Americans’ perspectives on DEI have become more polarized, the workload for international companies has only increased. “Whenever the wind blows one way, we have one kind of lawsuit, and then when the wind blows the other way, we have another kind of lawsuit,” said Katie Mehnert, who is chief executive officer of Houston-based workforce development company Ally Energy and has also worked at Shell. “It’s just a very disruptive approach to how to do business.” Top photo: Thomas Hutt Photographer: Shelby Tauber/Bloomberg. items.title: Microsoft outage disrupts businesses, governments globally
items.original_title: Microsoft outage disrupts businesses, governments globally
items.rss_title: Microsoft outage disrupts businesses, governments globally
items.rss_description: A more than 12-hour outage of Microsoft Outlook and Teams crippled communications for businesses and governments globally on Friday, forcing some organizations to revert to fax machines and halting at least one bond repurchase in Europe.
items.extracted_text: Microsoft said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant and that a broader rollout of software fixes was starting to stabilize the system. It said it was not aware of any malicious activity. Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings. It affected government agencies from Australia to Japan and the United States, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements. Organizations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were somewhat spared. The outage is one of the longest in Microsoft’s history and the second disruption to its services this year. Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online — its cloud-based email and scheduling hub — leaving unconnected applications operational. The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it. Microsoft shares fell 1.7% before the bell, lagging the broader market. They have gained roughly 8% so far this year. “The bigger worry is that this is not the first Microsoft 365 outage this year,” said Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at trading platform eToro. “If reliability starts to look like a recurring problem, it hands every IT department a reason to think twice before putting even more of their business in one provider’s hands.” Still, some analysts have questioned whether such incidents can push customers on to rivals due to the steep switching costs of replacing tools embedded so deeply in daily operations. Microsoft faced an outage with its 365 services in January this year and also in October last year. Last month, it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software, and a range of industries worldwide. A spokesperson for the U.K. government said it was working with Microsoft to find a solution for the outage that hit organizations such as the NHS and London’s Metropolitan Police. Lack of access to email and other services was impacting the Metropolitan Police’s ability to report some crimes online, though its ability to respond to calls was not affected. NHS said its local services were turning to alternate measures such as using IT systems or paper records. For businesses, the fallout was widespread. European exchange operator Euronext reported email disruptions, British insurer Aviva activated backups for its earnings calls and Danish shipping giant Maersk warned customers of delayed updates. American AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic also faced issues with Microsoft connectors, while Indian airlines IndiGo INGL.NS, Akasa Air and Air India said their email support services were impacted. The outage also disrupted fund management at Taiwanese securities firms, life insurers, and investment trust companies. One of the companies went as far as canceling a bond repurchase transaction, a source familiar with the situation told Reuters. Another Taiwanese financial company resorted to using fax to confirm trades, a second source said. In the U.S., electric truck maker Workhorse Group rescheduled its results on Thursday to Nov. 16, while Switzerland’s Richemont briefly delayed its first-half results announcement on Friday. In Australia, where the spy agency and federal police were among organizations caught in the outage, Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said Microsoft does not suspect a cyber attack. “The impact that they are dealing with … is very much on email systems,” the minister added. items.title: California comp medical reviews decline for first time since 2022
items.original_title: California comp medical reviews decline for first time since 2022
items.rss_title: California comp medical reviews decline for first time since 2022
items.rss_description: The number of independent medical reviews in California’s workers compensation system declined during the first nine months of 2026, marking the first decrease since 2022, according to a report released this week by the California Workers’ Compensation Institute.
items.extracted_text: The report found that 110,965 independent medical review decision letters were issued through September, down 3.1% from the same period in 2025. Despite the decline, review volume remained above comparable levels recorded from 2020 through 2024. Independent medical review physicians upheld 90.2% of utilization review denials and modifications, up from 89.8% in 2025. Pharmaceutical disputes continued to account for the largest share of reviews, representing 30.8% of decisions, followed by physical therapy at 13.2% and injections at 12.8%. Opioid disputes declined to 16.7% of pharmaceutical reviews, while the rate at which reviewers upheld opioid denials and modifications reached a record 95.7%. Dermatological drugs accounted for a record 25.9% of pharmaceutical disputes, more than double their 12.3% share in 2018. The report also found that a small group of physicians accounted for a disproportionate share of disputed medical services. The top 10% of physicians named in decision letters during the 12 months ending in September accounted for 84.5% of disputed service requests, while the top 1% accounted for 41.9%. The institute analyzed approximately 1.8 million independent medical review decision letters issued between 2015 and September 2026. items.extracted_text: California Earthquake Authority lowers pricing again for still $900m Ursa Re 2026-1 cat bond - Artemis.bm California Earthquake Authority lowers pricing again for still $900m Ursa Re 2026-1 cat bond - Artemis.bm California Earthquake Authority lowers pricing again for still $900m Ursa Re 2026-1 cat bond 12th November 2026 - Author: Jack Willard The California Earthquake Authority’s (CEA) new Ursa Re Ltd. (Series 2026-1) catastrophe bond remains at the upsized $900 million target, but pricing has been lowered again for the notes on offer, as the company targets strong execution with its latest cat bond deal, Artemis understands. The California Earthquake Authority (CEA) is one of the most consistent sponsors of catastrophe bonds, with this marking the 25th cat bond sponsorship we have tracked from the insurer. View details of every catastrophe bond sponsored by the CEA in the Artemis Deal Directory . Initially, the CEA was aiming to secure $600 million of reinsurance protection from this Ursa Re 2026-1 cat bond sponsorship. In our first update on this transaction, we learned that the CEA was looking to increase the amount of reinsurance limit from its latest deal, with Ursa Re Ltd. offering $900 million of notes across the two tranches of this Series 2026-1 cat bond issuance, a 50% increase from the initial $600 million target. At the same time, the CEA also looked to capitalise on investor appetite within the market, as the spread guidance for both notes on offer for this deal were reduced. We’re told that the upsized $900 million target remains, but CEA is still seeking to secure that protection at a more cost-effective rate, as the price guidance has been lowered once again for each of the tranches on offer. As we’ve previously said, at a $900 million issuance size, Artemis’ data shows that this new cat bond for the CEA is targeted to become the company’s largest since 2017 and the earthquake insurers second largest cat bond sponsorship ever. Ursa Re Ltd. continues to offer $900 million of earthquake reinsurance limit across the two tranches of cat bond notes on offer. These notes will provide the CEA with a roughly four-year source of fully-collateralized California earthquake reinsurance protection on an indemnity trigger and annual aggregate basis, which is the same trigger structure that CEA’s cat bonds have adopted in the past. What was a $350 million tranche of Series 2026-1 Class D notes are still targeted at their increased $500 million in size we understand. These Class D notes have an initial expected loss of 2.68% and they initially offered to cat bond investors with price guidance in a range from 4% to 4.5%, which was first lowered to between 3.75% to 4%, and we’re now told have been lowered to a revised range of 3.5% to 3.75%. What was initially a $250 million tranche of Series 2026-1 Class H of notes are still targeted at their increased $400 million in size. The Class H notes come with an initial expected loss of 6.35% and were first offered to cat bond investors with price guidance in a range from 8.5% to 9.5%, which was later revised to lower spread of 8.25% to 8.5%. We’re now told this price guidance has been lowered once again, to a revised range of 8% to 8.25%. We’ve previously said that we believe the Class H notes have the highest expected loss for any tranche of catastrophe bonds that we have seen sponsored by the CEA. The CEA looks set to meaningfully capitalise on catastrophe bond market conditions, in being able to secure 50% more fully-collateralized California earthquake reinsurance protection than originally sought. The decline in pricing is also no surprise given how cat bond issues have been executing of late across the market, as the space remains well-capitalised.
